analysis.one_liner: Requires lenders to show small businesses the true APR and total cost of financing offers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required lenders to disclose the true annual percentage rate on small business loans, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on June 15, 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the Truth in Lending Act — the same disclosure rules that apply to personal credit cards and mortgages — to loans and financing of $2.5 million or less made to small businesses. Lenders would have to show the annual percentage rate, all fees, payment amounts, and prepayment penalties in writing at the time of an offer, and could not charge a fee on a refinanced loan's old principal unless the business actually benefits. It would also give the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau authority over small business financing and require rules within two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses — the bakeries, contractors, truckers, and shops that take out loans, equipment financing, merchant cash advances, or factoring deals of $2.5 million or less. Today many of these products are marketed with a "factor rate" or flat fee that hides an annualized cost that can run to 60%, 100%, or more; the bill would force every offer to show a standard APR, the full payment schedule, and any prepayment penalties, making offers comparable before signing. It would also bar lenders from charging a new fee on the old balance when refinancing a fixed-fee loan unless there is a real benefit to the borrower.

how_it_helps.text: Lenders would have to disclose the annual percentage rate (APR), the amount actually received after withheld fees, payment amounts and frequency, the term, the itemized finance charge, prepayment costs, and any collateral requirements in writing at the time of a specific offer, displayed prominently so a business can compare options.

Sales-based financing (merchant cash advances) and factoring — products whose costs are usually quoted as rates or discounts rather than annualized percentages — would have to show an estimated APR, with the CFPB monitoring providers' sales projections for accuracy.

Lenders could not charge a fee on a loan's outstanding principal when refinancing or modifying a fixed-fee loan unless there is a tangible benefit to the small business, and any prepayment penalty triggered by refinancing with the same lender would count as part of the disclosed finance charge.

Other cost metrics could not be labeled a 'rate' unless they are the actual annual rate, and whenever a lender states a rate in writing it must state the APR with equal or greater prominence — closing the gap between a quoted '1.2 factor rate' and its true annual cost.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would have the same supervisory and enforcement authority over small business financing that it has over consumer financial products, and would have to issue final rules within 24 months, with the requirements taking effect 36 months after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Providers of small business financing — especially online lenders, merchant cash advance companies, and factoring firms that profit from opaque, high-cost structures — would bear compliance costs for new disclosures, face CFPB supervision, and could lose revenue where borrowers, able to see the true annual cost, switch to cheaper financing or decline the offer. Traditional banks already disclose APRs to consumers and would face fewer changes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online and high-cost small business lenders

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on all providers, including community banks and credit unions that already disclose APRs to consumers; smaller lenders would need new systems to compute APRs for sales-based and factoring products, where the annualized cost depends on estimates of a borrower's future sales that may prove wrong.

Some higher-risk borrowers — businesses with weak credit that online and subprime lenders serve when banks will not — could face fewer or more expensive offers if providers pull back from products whose true cost, once disclosed as an APR, is harder to sell.

The disclosure regime depends on CFPB rulemaking with a 24-month deadline and a 36-month delay before taking effect, so businesses would not see any change for years even if enacted, and the rules' final shape would be left to the Bureau.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the businesses borrowing the money, the benefits are concrete and immediate: a written, comparable APR on every offer, an itemized finance charge, and protection from being charged twice on a refinanced fixed-fee loan. The costs are real but standard for consumer credit already — lenders of every size have complied with APR disclosure on mortgages and credit cards for decades — and the main uncertainty is estimating APRs on sales-based products. The bill addresses a documented asymmetry: small business financing sits outside the Truth in Lending Act precisely because it is business credit, which leaves merchant cash advances and factoring largely undisclosed. On balance the benefits to borrowers outweigh the compliance burden, though the three-year implementation lag blunts the help.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Nydia Velázquez introduced the bill on June 15, 2023, joined by Representative Maxine Waters, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill drew one additional cosponsor in total, all Democrats, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in its action history through the end of the Congress.
Because bills do not carry over between Congresses, the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Small business lenders, particularly online lenders and merchant cash advance and factoring companies, are better off because the bill never advanced: their products remain outside the Truth in Lending Act's disclosure rules, and nothing stops them from continuing to quote costs as factor rates or flat fees instead of annual percentage rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost small business lenders kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats engaged — Velázquez, Waters, and one more Democratic cosponsor — but with just three names on the bill and no recorded opposition, no votes, or Republican statements in the record, the partisan shape cannot be measured; the bill simply never moved under Republican control of the House.

industries.industry: Online and merchant cash advance lenders
industries.note: These firms sell sales-based financing and short-term advances quoted as factor rates or flat fees rather than APRs; the bill would force an estimated APR on every offer and put them under CFPB supervision. Borrowers seeing a 60%+ annualized cost on paper could decline or shop around, cutting into a revenue model built on opaque pricing.

Factoring — buying a business's unpaid invoices at a discount — would for the first time require an estimated APR computed from the discount and payment due dates. This makes visible an annualized cost that the discount structure currently obscures.
Lease-financing deals would have to fold the purchase option price into a disclosed finance charge and show an APR, ending pricing structures where the end-of-lease buyout cost is hard to compare.

Consumer-facing banks already disclose APRs under the Truth in Lending Act and would face adjustment costs in extending that machinery to business products, but uniform disclosure favors lenders whose pricing is competitive and already transparent.
